Implacable
ĭm-plăk'ə-bəl
adj. (not to be appeased; refusing to be reconciled)
Latin implacabilis, from in-, not, and placare, to appease or pacify. The man who cannot be brought to peace, however the offence is confessed or the amends offered.

Biblical Definition

The word appears once, at the bottom of Romans 1: “Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” (Rom 1:31). Every term in that line is a negative — the passage is describing not the presence of vice so much as the absence of the things that make men human, and implacability is the refusal of the peace that reconciliation offers. The next verse shows how deep it goes: such men know the judgment of God and “have pleasure in them that do them” (Rom 1:32). Set against this the Lord's parable, where the forgiven servant takes his fellow by the throat and hears the question that answers implacability for ever: “Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?” (Mat 18:33). The wisdom from above is described in the exact opposite terms: “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits” (Jas 3:17). Easy to be intreated is the direct antonym of implacable; a Christian is to be a man whom an offending brother can approach. And the command is plainer still: “And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you” (Eph 4:32).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines implacable as not to be appeased or pacified; inexorable; stubborn or constant in enmity; and applied to passions, not to be subdued.

expand to see more

IMPLACABLE, a. [L. implacabilis; in and placabilis, from placo, to appease.] Not to be appeased; that cannot be pacified and rendered peaceable; inexorable; stubborn or constant in enmity.

2. Not to be appeased or subdued; as implacable hatred; implacable enmity.

IMPLACABLENESS, n. The quality of not being appeasable; inexorableness; irreconcilable enmity.

Without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful. Rom. i.

Key Scripture

Rom 1:31 — "Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful:"

Rom 1:32 — "Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them."

Mat 18:33 — "Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?"

Eph 4:32 — "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."

Modern Corruption

Refusing reconciliation is now defended as the protection of oneself, and a settled unwillingness to be entreated is presented as a virtue rather than named as the sin of Romans 1:31.

expand to see more

A vocabulary has grown up in which permanent estrangement is described as a wise arrangement: the offender is cut off, the door is closed, and the closing is spoken of as strength. Some of what that vocabulary addresses is real, and Scripture provides for it — a man is not obliged to entrust himself again to one who has not repented, Paul names those from whom we are to turn away, and the church has the power to put a man out. But there is a difference between withholding trust from an unrepentant man and being a man who cannot be entreated at all, and Romans 1:31 names the second as one of the marks of a mind given over. The test is simple and searching: if the offender came, confessed the thing plainly, and sought peace, would he find a door? Where the honest answer is no, the position is not prudence, it is implacability, and it stands in a list with covenantbreaking and the loss of natural affection.

James gives the Christian standard in a phrase our language has almost lost: the wisdom from above is easy to be intreated. That does not mean gullible, and it does not mean soft on sin — the same verse puts first pure before then peaceable, and the order is not negotiable. It means approachable; a man to whom the person in the wrong can come. The reason the New Testament presses this so hard is not that offences are small but that the Christian's own case was hopeless. The servant in Matthew 18 was forgiven ten thousand talents and took his fellow by the throat for a hundred pence, and the Lord's question is the only argument the passage needs. A man who has truly reckoned what he was forgiven at the cross has lost the standing from which implacability can be maintained.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek aspondos (G786) in the Received Text at Romans 1:31, admitting no truce; contrasted with eupeithes (G2138), easy to be intreated, and eleemon (G1655), merciful.

expand to see more

Greek aspondos (G786) — without libation, admitting no terms of peace; rendered implacable at Romans 1:31 and trucebreakers at 2 Timothy 3:3.

Greek aneleemon (G415) — unmerciful, without pity; the companion word closing the same verse; Romans 1:31.

Greek eupeithes (G2138) — easily persuaded, easy to be intreated; the mark of the wisdom that is from above; James 3:17.

Greek katallasso (G2644) — to reconcile, to change from enmity to friendship; the work God did toward us in Christ; 2 Corinthians 5:18-19.

Greek splagchnizomai (G4697) — to be moved with compassion in the inward parts; the pity the unforgiving servant had received and would not give; Matthew 18:27.

Usage

"“Without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” — the negatives that describe a mind given over."

"“Easy to be intreated” — the direct antonym, and a mark of wisdom from above."

"“Even as I had pity on thee” — the question that ends every argument for an unopenable door."
